source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 4 (Physiology), section 4.1 (Seed germination physiology). No elibrary URL visible.
text: Rice seed germination follows a three-stage physiological model (Takahashi, 1962; Bewley and Black, 1985). Stage 1 (imbibition) is rapid, purely physical water absorption, raising seed moisture to roughly 30% of seed weight within hours - this stage does not yet require living cell activity. Stage 2 is a lag phase during which biochemical activity begins: stored starch in the endosperm is broken down by seed enzymes into sugars (glucose, sucrose, and smaller amounts of raffinose and fructose) that fuel the growing embryo. Stage 3 is visible growth - root (radicle) and shoot (plumule/coleoptile) emergence. A distinctive feature of rice among cereal crops is that it can germinate under low-oxygen (anaerobic/flooded) conditions, unlike most other cereals which require aerobic conditions to germinate - under flooding, the coleoptile can elongate before root growth begins, whereas under normal aerobic conditions the root typically emerges first, within about 24-48 hours. This anaerobic-germination ability is part of why rice can be established via direct seeding into standing water.
